catalog_citation: Regueira, Xosé L. 1996. Galician. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 26(2): 119-122 (Illustrations of the IPA). Cambridge Core PDF.
catalog_quote: Stress in Galician may fall on any of the last three syllables of a word. If a word has a closed syllable in final position, stress usually falls on that syllable, e.g. final [fiˈnal] 'end', roncón [roŋˈkoŋ] 'pipe in a bagpipe', armar [arˈmar] 'to arm'. In certain loans and learned words stress may be on the penultimate syllable, as in revólver [reˈβolβer] 'revolver', dolmen [ˈdɔlmɛŋ] 'dolmen', útil [ˈutil] 'useful'. If there is a final open syllable in a word, stress will normally fall on the penultimate syllable, e.g. casa [ˈkɑsa] 'house', home [ˈɔme] 'man', carballo [kɑrˈβaʎo] 'oak', edificio [eðiˈfiθjo] 'building'. However, some words end in a stressed vowel, e.g. avó [aˈβo] 'grandfather', alá [aˈla] 'over there'. sources.citation: Saavedra Carballido, Jesús M. 2026. A versificación anisosilábica en galego de Rosalía de Castro. Verba: Anuario Galego de Filoloxía 53: 1-52. doi:10.15304/verba.53.9253
sources.quote: E polo que di respecto ás lingüísticas, non nos interesan os aspectos fonéticos, senón só os fonolóxicos: entre eles, nomeadamente, cal é a sonoridade e a abertura de cada fonema; cales son as palabras tónicas e cales as átonas; se as palabras son agudas, graves, esdrúxulas ou sobresdrúxulas; cales son, en calquera palabra, as sílabas nucleares e cales, nas palabras polisilábicas, as sílabas que podemos denominar ancilares (quer prenucelares quer posnucleares). [fn. 13:] Para sabermos cales son as palabras tónicas e cales as átonas, e cales son as sílabas nucleares e ancilares de cada unha delas (i. e., as normalmente prominentes e non prominentes na cadea falada), debemos consultar as gramáticas e os dicionarios existentes.
sources.locator: p. 18 and fn. 13; also p. 19 (lexical words verb, noun, adjective, adverb 'sempre tónicos'; every word has one nuclear syllable)
sources.note: marginal: Metrical analysis of Rosalía de Castro's anisosyllabic Galician verse using metrical patterns and realisation rules grounded in the language's phonology; stress data only incidental to versification.

sources.citation: Dubert García, Francisco. 2012. Historia de la palabra, variación dialectal, propiedades morfosintácticas y acento en el verbo regular gallego. Vox Romanica 71: 197-228. (CC BY 4.0; Minerva USC hdl 10347/33780)
sources.quote: p.197-198: apart from passing remarks in grammars (Álvarez/Regueira/Monteagudo 1986:305; Álvarez/Xove 2002:245) only Parafita Couto 2007 treats Galician verb stress. p.204-205: the most common pattern in the regular conjugation is 'acento en la penúltima sílaba', proposed as default V[σ' σ]w, with listed exceptions (infinitive cantar, 1sg cantei, 1/2pl cantásemos/cantásedes antepenult, futures). p.225: 'la posición del acento en el verbo gallego no es sensible a la cantidad' (2pl.imp cantade, cantai, cantá all stress the theme vowel regardless of suffix shape); stress position is anchored to m
sources.locator: pp. 197-198 (state of research), pp. 204-205 (default pattern (6)), pp. 225-226 (Conclusiones)
sources.note: Only open stress-specific study of Galician found; shows verb stress is quantity-insensitive and morphologically anchored (default penult), supporting lexical over a weight-driven reading; downloaded now.

sources.citation: Hernández Hudson, Erika, Antje Muntendam & Carolina González. 2026. The intonation of yes-no questions in Galician. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 56: e9, 1-31. doi:10.1017/S0025100326100954
sources.locator: p. 2; also p. 9 (target items: penultimate stress 77/80, antepenultimate 3/80, final-stress words avoided) and p. 10 (nuclear pitch accent = last stressed syll…
sources.note: The article is an acoustic study of sentence intonation: Galician yes-no questions end mostly in falls (57%, chiefly H+L* L%) but often in rises (43%, chiefly L+H* H%), with falls favoured by women, older and Galician-dominant speakers. On word stress it only restates Regueira 1996 (the catalog's own source): stress is lexically placed on the final, penultimate or antepenultimate syllable, which matches the entry's lexical kind; no lexical tone is mentioned.
sources.venue: Journal of the International Phonetic Association

sources.citation: Rodríguez-Vázquez, Rosalía & Roseano, Paolo. 2022. L2 rhythm acquisition and rhythmic transfer in Galician learners of English: A pilot study. Loquens 9(1-2): e087. doi:10.3989/loquens.2022.087
sources.locator: pp. 3, 5; results p. 6 ("GAL is indeed syllable-timed (like Central Peninsular Spanish), while SBE is stress-timed")
sources.note: The article measures speech rhythm, not word stress: Galician L1 readings score as syllable-timed on all five duration metrics, and Galician learners' English lies between Galician and British English, closer to English at C1 than at B1. It says nothing about where word stress falls in Galician or about tone, and explicitly leaves stress, pitch and intensity to future work, so it neither confirms nor changes the catalog's lexical-stress entry.

sources.citation: Cajiao, Alba Aguete. 2025. The Unstressed Vowel Reduction of Galician. Languages 10(1): 16. doi:10.3390/languages10010016
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.note: Acoustic study of Galician unstressed vowels in semi-spontaneous speech from six young women: unstressed vowels are reduced by two mechanisms, raising and centralization, and the reduction does not depend on vowel duration, so the author treats it as grammar-controlled rather than mechanical. It adds unstressed-vowel reduction as a phonetic correlate of lexical stress but states nothing (in the abstract) about the position or type of the stress itself, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the entry's empty rule.
